ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: No papers appeared to involve live data collection requiring an ethics approval statement.
ethics_check.report: We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 858 columns across 106 data files.
#### Issues Identified

78 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 106 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

**`os.chdir()` in the code**
**1 script calls `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

info.title: Most coronial recommendations in Australia have no published response: a national analysis of findings and agency responses

author.affiliation:
Independent researcher
								
									Finley
									New South Wales
									Australia

text.text: Version 3.
This version replaces versions 1 (14 February 2026) and 2 (22 April 2026), whose compliance results are withdrawn.

Those versions read many Victorian responses only as their AustLII index pages, so they described most Victorian responses as administrative cover letters, and they classified responses with a rule-based classifier that agreed poorly with blinded human coding (kappa 0.17).
They also stated that the Queensland Coroners Act requires a ministerial response and that the Victorian Act does not prescribe the content of a response; neither is correct.

This version reextracts every affected document, retrieves the responses listed on Victorian index pages, classifies responses with a language model validated against blinded coding, and describes the response law from the current official texts.
Results remain provisional until the last 10 of 110 Victorian records can be retrieved.
Coroners are among the few officials whose job includes saying how the next death could be prevented.
In every Australian jurisdiction they may recommend changes to policy, practice or law (table 2).
text.formatted: In every Australian jurisdiction they may recommend changes to policy, practice or law (table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Studies of Victorian recommendations and of river drowning found that most specify a countermeasure and the level at which it should act, though many rely on administrative controls rather than stronger measures 1, 2 , and recent work has mapped the themes of recommendations to guide prevention 3 .
text.formatted: Studies of Victorian recommendations and of river drowning found that most specify a countermeasure and the level at which it should act, though many rely on administrative controls rather than stronger measures <ref type="bibr">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2</ref> , and recent work has mapped the themes of recommendations to guide prevention 3 .

text.text: A recommendation prevents nothing until someone acts on it, however, and evidence on what happens next is thin.

In England and Wales, where recipients of a Prevention of Future Deaths report must reply, topic-specific case series find a published response for only 40% to 78% of reports or report recipients [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9] [10] [11].
text.formatted: In England and Wales, where recipients of a Prevention of Future Deaths report must reply, topic-specific case series find a published response for only 40% to 78% of reports or report recipients <ref type="bibr">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[11]</ref>.

text.text: What happens to a recommendation once it leaves the court depends on where it was made (table 2).
text.formatted: What happens to a recommendation once it leaves the court depends on where it was made (table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Four jurisdictions impose a statutory duty to respond.
In Victoria a public entity must reply within three months with "a statement of action (if any) that has, is or will be taken", and the coroner must publish the reply online 12 .
text.formatted: In Victoria a public entity must reply within three months with "a statement of action (if any) that has, is or will be taken", and the coroner must publish the reply online <ref type="bibr">12</ref> .

text.text: South Australia, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory route responses to Parliament, the Legislative Assembly or the Attorney-General 13-15 .
Queensland's Act requires the coroner to send comments to government and publish them, but not that anyone reply 16 .
text.formatted: Queensland's Act requires the coroner to send comments to government and publish them, but not that anyone reply <ref type="bibr">16</ref> .

text.text: Its published responses rest on an administrative arrangement introduced in 2008 17, 18 .
text.formatted: Its published responses rest on an administrative arrangement introduced in 2008 <ref type="bibr">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr">18</ref> .

text.text: New South Wales relies on a Premier's memorandum asking agencies to report within six months 19 , and Western Australia and Tasmania have no response requirement 20, 21 .
text.formatted: New South Wales relies on a Premier's memorandum asking agencies to report within six months <ref type="bibr">19</ref> , and Western Australia and Tasmania have no response requirement <ref type="bibr">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr">21</ref> .

text.text: The Victorian and Queensland Acts were amended in 2026, after the study period, without changing these provisions.
Australian evidence on responses comes from single jurisdictions or single death types.

In Victoria's first years under s 72, recipient organisations reported implementing 37% of recommendations and rejecting 27% 22 , and only 44% of written responses said explicitly whether action had been or would be taken 23 .
text.formatted: In Victoria's first years under s 72, recipient organisations reported implementing 37% of recommendations and rejecting 27% 22 , and only 44% of written responses said explicitly whether action had been or would be taken <ref type="bibr">23</ref> .

text.text: A national study of recommendations after the homicide of older adults found a response for 27 of 29 recommendations, most of them supported 24 .
text.formatted: A national study of recommendations after the homicide of older adults found a response for 27 of 29 recommendations, most of them supported <ref type="bibr">24</ref> .

text.text: Recent work has applied language models to national collections of coronial reports, but to the circumstances of death rather than to responses 25, 26 .
text.formatted: Recent work has applied language models to national collections of coronial reports, but to the circumstances of death rather than to responses <ref type="bibr">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr">26</ref> .

text.text: No study has measured, across all jurisdictions and causes of death, how often a recommendation receives a published response and what that response says.

We used the national open collection of coronial findings and responses to estimate, for each Australian jurisdiction, the proportion of findings with recommendations that have a published agency response and the proportion of responses that accept the recommendations, and to examine which characteristics of the death are associated with acceptance.

We enumerated every document in the coronial databases of the Australasian Legal Information Institute (AustLII) Coronial Law Library in February 2026 27, 28 , which hold findings from all eight Australian jurisdictions and agency responses from seven (the Australian Capital Territory has no response database).
text.formatted: We enumerated every document in the coronial databases of the Australasian Legal Information Institute (AustLII) Coronial Law Library in February 2026 <ref type="bibr">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr">28</ref> , which hold findings from all eight Australian jurisdictions and agency responses from seven (the Australian Capital Territory has no response database).

text.text: The findings databases held 9,924 records, two of them duplicates.
Of the 9,922 findings, 9,831 had usable text (37 were under 200 characters and 54 were empty).
The response databases held 2,064 documents.
Text was extracted from HTML and PDF documents, with optical character recognition for scanned pages.
An audit of every PDF found that the original extraction had read only the text layer of mixed documents; 741 PDFs (158 findings and 583 responses) were re-extracted page by page.
Most of the affected responses were Victorian: AustLII stores many Victorian responses as an index page followed by scanned agency letters.

For 473 such records the letters were already on disk; 110 records held only the index page, and we retrieved the listed responses from the Coroners Court of Victoria website and the Internet Archive, accepting a document only when its text named the deceased.
Responses were retrieved for 100 of the 110.

AustLII publishes what each court supplies, so the corpus is the public record of the coronial system rather than all reportable deaths, and we expect it to be enriched for inquests and for cases with recommendations.

Responses were linked to findings by court reference numbers where available (Victoria, Queensland, Tasmania and the Northern Territory) and otherwise by the deceased's name and year (New South Wales, Western Australia and South Australia).
Documents without a usable name were not namematched (table S1).

text.text: Agency responses counted, as did 20 documents showing that a response existed but whose text was unavailable (including the 10 outstanding Victorian records).
Court tables recording that a response was awaited, not required or not received did not count.

There are two co-primary response measures: the proportion of findings with recommendations that have at least one counting response over all years, and the same proportion within each jurisdiction's response-database years (from the first to the last year in which the database holds a counting response) for findings up to 2023, so that every finding had at least two years to be answered.
The second was added after the first results were seen, when it became clear that the databases cover different periods (table 1).

text.text: Each response was classified by a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) using a prompt written from the author's coding definitions and fixed before testing, under a dated protocol written before each step and deposited with the analysis code 29 .
text.formatted: Each response was classified by a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) using a prompt written from the author's coding definitions and fixed before testing, under a dated protocol written before each step and deposited with the analysis code <ref type="bibr">29</ref> .

text.text: The model assigned the document type and one of seven positions: implemented, already implemented, partially accepted, under consideration, noted, not supported, or unclassifiable.
Accepted means implemented, already implemented or partially accepted.
These categories record the position stated in the response, not whether anything changed in practice.
The prompt and model were tested once against 100 responses that the author had coded blind to any machine label.
Seven-category agreement was kappa 0.81 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.90) and binary acceptance agreement 0.73 (0.50 to 0.91), against 0.17 and 0.10 for a rule-based classifier tested first (tables S3 and S4).
text.formatted: Seven-category agreement was kappa 0.81 (95% CI 0.71 to 0.90) and binary acceptance agreement 0.73 (0.50 to 0.91), against 0.17 and 0.10 for a rule-based classifier tested first (tables <ref type="table">S3</ref> and <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Because only 10 of the 90 classifiable test responses were not accepted, the author coded 40 more from the full corpus, blind to the model's labels: 30 the model labelled not accepted and 10 accepted.
The author agreed in 25 of 30 (95% CI 65% to 94%) and 10 of 10 (69% to 100%); weighted to the corpus, binary accuracy was 97.2% (table S5).
text.formatted: The author agreed in 25 of 30 (95% CI 65% to 94%) and 10 of 10 (69% to 100%); weighted to the corpus, binary accuracy was 97.2% (table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: Where a finding had more than one counting response, its outcome was the position taken by most of its classifiable responses, with an exact tie counted as partially accepted (the rule the author's coding definitions apply to a single letter answering several recommendations).
This rule was fixed before the models were refitted; accepted if any response accepts, and accepted only if all do, are reported as sensitivity analyses (table S6).
text.formatted: This rule was fixed before the models were refitted; accepted if any response accepts, and accepted only if all do, are reported as sensitivity analyses (table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Indigenous status, medication involvement and custodial or institutional settings (psychiatric facility, prison or other correctional setting, police custody) were flagged by layered regular expressions on the text of the findings (table S7).
text.formatted: Indigenous status, medication involvement and custodial or institutional settings (psychiatric facility, prison or other correctional setting, police custody) were flagged by layered regular expressions on the text of the findings (table <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: These flags mark what a finding mentions, not the place of death or a coded attribute of the deceased.
A post hoc sensitivity analysis refitted the acceptance model with narrower flags that excluded community crisis teams, police watch houses and remand.
Proportions are given with Wilson 95% confidence intervals.
Whether a response accepted the recommendations was modelled by logistic regression on jurisdiction (reference New South Wales), year, log document length, and the case flags.

Because every Northern Territory response was accepted, the models used Firth's penalised likelihood with profile-likelihood confidence intervals 30, 31 ; an ordinary model excluding the Northern Territory is reported as a sensitivity analysis.

text.text: All documents are court records already published by the courts.
The study involved no contact with families and reports no names or case details, so formal ethics review was not sought and consent was not applicable.
The documents remain subject to the terms of AustLII and the courts and are not redistributed.
Some findings concern the deaths of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

No Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander organisation or community was involved in the design or interpretation of this analysis, which falls short of the collective benefit and authority to control set out in the CARE and Maiam nayri Wingara principles 33, 34 .
text.formatted: No Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander organisation or community was involved in the design or interpretation of this analysis, which falls short of the collective benefit and authority to control set out in the CARE and Maiam nayri Wingara principles <ref type="bibr">33,</ref> <ref type="bibr">34</ref> .

text.text: Results are therefore reported only in aggregate, and the analysis draws no conclusions about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
Of 9,831 findings, 4,480 (45.6%; 95% CI 44.6% to 46.6%) contained recommendations, ranging from 28.9% in Western Australia to 70.1% in South Australia (table 1).
Only 1,309 of the 4,480 findings with recommendations (29.2%) had a counting response in the AustLII record.

The proportion was highest in Western Australia (54.4%), New South Wales (47.4%) and Victoria (42.1%), and lowest in South Australia (11.8%), the Northern Territory (9.7%), Tasmania (5.0%) and the Australian Capital Territory, which has no response database.

In New South Wales a further 31 findings (7.1% of those with recommendations) had only a court table recording that a response was awaited; counting any linked document, the New South Wales figure would be 55.2% (table S9).

text.text: Victoria's holds responses published from 2009 to 2021, Tasmania's from 2015 and the Northern Territory's from 2019.
Within each jurisdiction's database years, 1,242 of 3,392 findings with recommendations (36.6%; 35.0% to 38.3%) had a counting response.
The order changed little except in the Northern Territory, where the rate rose from 9.7% to 42.9% (12 of 28).
South Australia (15.2%) and Tasmania (5.8%) remained low (figure 1).
text.formatted: South Australia (15.2%) and Tasmania (5.8%) remained low (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In all, 1,541 findings had a counting response with a classifiable outcome.
They include 244 findings in which the recommendation detector had found no recommendation, and acceptance was the same with or without them (85.4%).
Of the 1,541, 1,316 (85.4%; 83.5% to 87.1%) accepted the recommendations: 64.0% were implemented, 6.9% already implemented and 14.5% partially accepted.
A further 8.3% were under consideration, 5.0% not supported and 1.3% noted.
Acceptance ranged from 65.0% (56.1% to 72.9%) in Western Australia, where many responses left recommendations under consideration, to 100% of the 22 Northern Territory findings (table 1).
In the adjusted model (figure 2), acceptance was lower in Victoria (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.50) and Western Australia (0.12, 0.06 to 0.21) than in New South Wales.
text.formatted: In the adjusted model (figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>), acceptance was lower in Victoria (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.50) and Western Australia (0.12, 0.06 to 0.21) than in New South Wales.

text.text: Findings that mentioned a psychiatric unit (2.02, 1.25 to 3.35) or a prison or other correctional setting (1.78, 1.12 to 2.92) were more likely to receive an accepting response.
A mention of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander identity was not associated with acceptance (0.78, 0.46 to 1.37), nor was year (0.98 per year, 0.94 to 1.03).
Both facility associations survived false discovery rate correction, along with 27 other tests (29 of 41 in all).  S7).
text.formatted: Both facility associations survived false discovery rate correction, along with 27 other tests (29 of 41 in all).  <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: The facility associations held under the alternative rules for findings with several responses (psychiatric facility 2.11 if any response accepted and 1.61 if all had to; prison 1.83 and 1.59) and with the narrower flags (post hoc: 1.81, 1.11 to 3.05; and 1.71, 1.07 to 2.82).
Excluding the Northern Territory changed no other odds ratio by more than 0.08.
The jurisdiction contrasts were sensitive to the reference group, which had only 17 non-accepting findings: under the strictest rule, the Victorian odds ratio was 0.51 (0.31 to 0.82).

text.text: Changes after the period, in 2026: Victoria's Justice Legislation Further Amendment (Miscellaneous) Act 2026 added powers to discontinue some investigations and changed who may apply to set findings aside, and Queensland's Justice and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2026 amended the provisions on findings and comments (ss 45 to 47, from 29 October 2026); neither altered the response arrangements shown.

Across Australia, fewer than a third of coronial findings with recommendations had a published agency response on AustLII, and little more than a third even within the years the response databases cover.
When a response was published, it usually accepted the recommendations: 85% of findings with a classifiable response were implemented, already implemented or partially accepted.
The weak point in this record is therefore less what agencies say than whether anyone can see that they said it.
The proportion of findings with a published response did not line up with the statutory duties in table 2.

Within the databases' years, Victoria (a duty to respond and to publish) and New South Wales and Western Australia (no statutory duty) all had published responses for half or more of findings with recommendations.
South Australia, which requires ministers to report to Parliament, reached 15%, and Tasmania, with no requirement, 6%.
Most Northern Territory findings with recommendations (164 of 217) predate its response database, which begins in 2019; within that period 12 of 28 had a response.
The
Australian Capital Territory, despite its tabling duty, has no response database at all.
A duty to respond and a place where responses can be found are separate design choices, and only the second lets families, researchers and other agencies learn what happened to a recommendation.
The gap also shows within jurisdictions.

Victoria's Act requires online publication, yet no Victorian response after 2021 is on AustLII, and Queensland's court publishes responses beside its findings 18 while only 28.5% of Queensland findings with recommendations have one on AustLII.
The figures here are a floor for what exists and an accurate count of what the national collection holds.

The same pattern appears in England and Wales, where responses are mandatory and yet case series across topics find a published response for 40% to 78% of reports or report recipients [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] ; larger organisations respond more often than smaller ones 35 , and many responses never enter the public domain 36 .

text.text: A response that exists only in a departmental file cannot inform prevention elsewhere.
Stated acceptance was high and fairly uniform, with two exceptions.

In Western Australia a third of findings with a response were not accepted, mostly because the response left the recommendation under consideration, possibly because responses there are published before a decision is made.
Victorian responses accepted less often than those in New South Wales (81.8% against 94.1%).

One explanation, which these data cannot test, is selection: where responding is voluntary, the replies that are written and published may lean towards acceptance, while a mandatory regime also captures those that decline or merely note a recommendation.
The contrast narrowed (odds ratio 0.51) when only findings whose every response accepted counted as accepted.
High stated acceptance is not the same as implementation.

Victorian organisations surveyed directly reported implementing 37% of recommendations 22 , and fewer than half of Victorian responses stated plainly what would be done 23 ; in the older-adult homicide study, most recommendations were supported, and over half had been implemented or partly implemented when the study was done 24 .
text.formatted: Victorian organisations surveyed directly reported implementing 37% of recommendations 22 , and fewer than half of Victorian responses stated plainly what would be done 23 ; in the older-adult homicide study, most recommendations were supported, and over half had been implemented or partly implemented when the study was done <ref type="bibr">24</ref> .

text.text: A government review reported most recommendations of the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody implemented 37 , a conclusion disputed using later coronial findings 38 .
Our measure records the position an agency took on paper, and should be read as an upper bound on change in practice.

Findings that mentioned a psychiatric unit or a prison were more likely to receive an accepting response, after adjustment, under each rule for findings with several responses and with narrower flags.

The flags record a mention, not necessarily the place of death, but these are settings run or closely regulated by government, where the agency that receives a recommendation is usually the one able to act on it and deaths attract sustained scrutiny.

A mention of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander identity, which the flag detects through identity terms, organisations or context such as remote community or customary law, was not associated with acceptance once jurisdiction was taken into account.
The null result says nothing about whether accepted recommendations were implemented.
This is the first analysis of published responses across all Australian jurisdictions and causes of death, with a classifier fixed before testing and validated twice against blinded human coding.

AustLII holds what courts supply and keeps adding documents, including some dated before the enumeration, so findings are enriched for inquests and the response measures count published responses, not all responses.

In New South Wales, where linkage relied on names, 57% of response documents could be linked and the links were not checked by hand; of the 291 unlinked, 207 named a person with no New South Wales finding on AustLII, 57 had no usable name, and only 22 may be missed links (table S1).

text.text: Ten Victorian and four New South Wales responses known to exist were unavailable; they count as responses but not towards acceptance.
The classifier's errors in the blinded check ran one way, so acceptance is if anything slightly understated.
Case characteristics came from text, not coded data.
The within-database measure was defined after the first results were seen and uses the years each database holds responses as a proxy for when they were collected.
Finally, the jurisdiction contrasts rest on a reference group with few non-accepting findings.
Australia lacks a single place where a recommendation and its response can be read together.
A national register, built on Victorian and Queensland publication practice, would make the response rate visible and allow follow-up of implementation, not only of stated intent.
The methods used here can be rerun as findings are published, so such a register could report response and acceptance rates routinely.
In Australia a coronial recommendation is more likely to go unanswered in public than to be refused.
Making responses findable, and then checking what happened, would do more for prevention than more evidence that agencies agree.
